anchor: Wave quantities and phase > Displacement and amplitude > Worked Example 1: Determining displacement and amplitude: "Amplitude is measured from the equilibrium line to a peak or trough, never from peak to trough."
title: Identifying Amplitude and Instantaneous Displacement
action: Select the option that correctly states the amplitude and instantaneous displacement from the given description of a water wave.
prompt: A floating buoy oscillates between a high point of +0.80 m and a low point of -0.80 m relative to calm water. At time t = 2.0 s, the buoy is at +0.40 m. What are the wave's amplitude and the buoy's instantaneous displacement at t = 2.0 s?

feedback.A: Correct. Amplitude is the maximum displacement from equilibrium (0.80 m). Instantaneous displacement is the signed position at that specific moment (+0.40 m).
feedback.B: Incorrect. 1.60 m is the peak-to-peak distance from +0.80 m to -0.80 m, which is twice the amplitude. Amplitude is measured from equilibrium to a peak.
feedback.C: Incorrect. This reverses the quantities. The maximum displacement from equilibrium is the amplitude (0.80 m), while the displacement at t = 2.0 s is the instantaneous value (+0.40 m).
feedback.D: Incorrect. The buoy is at height +0.40 m, so the instantaneous displacement is positive (+0.40 m), not negative.

anchor: Wave quantities and phase > Period and frequency > Worked Example 2: Calculating frequency from timing data: "Dividing the total duration by the number of complete oscillations yields the period."
title: Determining Period and Frequency from Multi-Cycle Timing
action: Select the correct period and frequency for a wave source where 50 complete oscillations are timed over 2.5 seconds.
prompt: A loudspeaker cone completes 50 full vibration cycles in 2.5 s. What are the period and the frequency of the sound wave emitted?

feedback.A: Correct. Period T = total time / number of cycles = 2.5 s / 50 = 0.050 s. Frequency f = 1 / T = 1 / 0.050 s = 20 Hz.
feedback.B: Incorrect. This inverts the definitions by calculating cycles per second as the period and seconds per cycle as the frequency.
feedback.C: Incorrect. The period is correct, but the frequency is the reciprocal of period (1 / 0.050 s = 20 Hz), not the total number of cycles.
feedback.D: Incorrect. This incorrectly takes the total time of 2.5 s as 0.025 s. Dividing 2.5 s by 50 cycles gives T = 0.050 s.

anchor: Wave quantities and phase > Reading wave graphs: space versus time > Worked Example 4: Extracting wave quantities from dual graphs: "Check the horizontal axis label before reading repeating wave intervals."
title: Distinguishing Displacement-Distance and Displacement-Time Graphs
action: Select the statement that correctly identifies what can be directly extracted from the horizontal repeat distance of each graph.
prompt: You are given two sinusoidal wave graphs: Graph P has distance x on the horizontal axis, while Graph Q has time t on the horizontal axis. Which quantities are directly obtained from the horizontal repeat lengths of P and Q?

options.text: Graph P gives wavelength; Graph Q gives period.
Graph P gives period; Graph Q gives wavelength.

feedback.A: Correct. A displacement-distance graph is a spatial snapshot where one cycle repeat equals the wavelength. A displacement-time graph shows a single particle's history where one cycle repeat equals the period.
feedback.B: Incorrect. This reverses the horizontal axes. Distance in metres cannot represent period in seconds, and time in seconds cannot represent wavelength in metres.
feedback.C: Incorrect. A time axis (Graph Q) represents elapsed time, not spatial distance, so it gives the period T rather than the wavelength.
feedback.D: Incorrect. A distance axis (Graph P) represents spatial position along the wave, not time, so it gives the wavelength lambda rather than the period.

anchor: Wave quantities and phase > What is phase? > Worked Example 5: Determining phase relationships: "Two particles are in phase only if their displacements and velocity directions match exactly."
title: Evaluating Phase Criteria: Displacement and Velocity Direction
action: Select the pair of particles that are in phase on a progressive transverse wave.
prompt: Four particles along a transverse wave have the following instantaneous states: Particle 1 has displacement +y_0 moving upward. Particle 2 has displacement +y_0 moving downward. Particle 3 has displacement -y_0 moving upward. Particle 4 has displacement +y_0 moving upward, located one full wavelength from Particle 1. Which two particles are in phase?

feedback.A: Correct. Particles 1 and 4 have identical displacement (+y_0) and are moving in the identical direction (upward). Separated by one full wavelength, they are in phase.
feedback.B: Incorrect. While Particles 1 and 2 have equal displacement (+y_0), they move in opposite directions (one upward, one downward). They are not in phase.
feedback.C: Incorrect. Particles 1 and 3 have opposite displacements (+y_0 and -y_0). Being in phase requires both identical displacement and identical velocity direction.
feedback.D: Incorrect. Particles 2 and 3 differ in displacement and move in opposite directions.

anchor: Wave quantities and phase > Quantitative phase difference > Worked Example 6: Phase difference from spatial separation: "Phase difference equals the path separation divided by wavelength multiplied by a full circle angle."
title: Calculating Phase Difference from Spatial Separation
action: Select the correct phase difference between two points separated by 0.50 m on a wave of wavelength 2.0 m.
prompt: A progressive wave has a wavelength of 2.0 m. What is the phase difference between two points along the wave separated by a distance of 0.50 m?

feedback.A: Correct. The cycle fraction is Delta x / lambda = 0.50 m / 2.0 m = 0.25. The phase difference is 0.25 x 360 degrees = 90 degrees, or 0.25 x 2 pi rad = pi/2 rad.
feedback.B: Incorrect. 45 degrees corresponds to an eighth of a cycle (0.125 lambda = 0.25 m). Here the separation is 0.50 m, which is one quarter of the 2.0 m wavelength.
feedback.C: Incorrect. 180 degrees corresponds to half a wavelength (1.0 m). Here the separation is 0.50 m (lambda / 4).
feedback.D: Incorrect. 0.25 is the dimensionless cycle fraction (Delta x / lambda). To find phase difference, you must multiply by 360 degrees or 2 pi radians.

anchor: Wave quantities and phase > Quantitative phase difference > Worked Example 7: Phase difference between two wave traces: "A temporal time lag translates directly to an angular phase difference across one period."
title: Determining Phase Difference from Wave Trace Time Shifts
action: Select the correct phase difference and time shift relation for two identical waves of period 4.0 ms shifted by 1.0 ms.
prompt: Wave X has a period of 4.0 ms. A second wave Y is identical in amplitude and frequency but is shifted in time so that its crest occurs 1.0 ms after the crest of wave X. What is the phase difference between wave X and wave Y?

feedback.A: Correct. The time shift is Delta t = 1.0 ms and the period is T = 4.0 ms. The cycle fraction is Delta t / T = 1.0 / 4.0 = 0.25. The phase difference is 0.25 x 360 degrees = 90 degrees (or pi/2 rad).
feedback.B: Incorrect. 60 degrees corresponds to a time shift of one sixth of a period (Delta t = T / 6 approx 0.67 ms). Here the shift is 1.0 ms, which is one quarter of 4.0 ms.
feedback.C: Incorrect. 180 degrees corresponds to half a period (2.0 ms), which would mean the waves are in antiphase.
feedback.D: Incorrect. 250 Hz is the frequency of the wave (f = 1 / 4.0 ms = 250 Hz), not the phase difference. Phase difference must be expressed in angular units (degrees or radians).
